lesson.title: Meet Python: A Language Designed to Be Read
lesson.summary: Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language known for readable syntax, dynamic typing, and a huge standard library, and it will be the language used throughout the rest of this course.
lesson.body:
Python was created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991, and it has since become one of the most widely used programming languages in the world, popular in web development, data science, automation, and education. Part of Python's appeal is a deliberate design philosophy that values code readability. Python's creators believed that code is read far more often than it is written, so the language was built so that Python code tends to look similar to how a person might describe an algorithm in plain, structured English.

The clearest sign of this philosophy is how Python defines blocks of code. Many programming languages use curly braces to mark where a block, such as the body of an if statement or a function, begins and ends. Python instead uses indentation itself as syntax. The lines inside a function or an if statement must be indented consistently, and that indentation is not just a style preference, it is how the interpreter determines which lines belong together. This is different from languages like Compiled vs Interpreted's earlier example in C, where braces mark blocks and indentation is only there for human readability.

Consider this short Python function:

def greet(name):
    if name:
        print("Hello, " + name)
    else:
        print("Hello, stranger")

greet("Ava")

Tracing this by hand: calling greet("Ava") binds the parameter name to the string "Ava" inside the function. The if name: line checks whether name is truthy, and a non-empty string is always truthy in Python, so the interpreter runs the indented line under if, which concatenates "Hello, " with "Ava" and prints Hello, Ava. The indented else block is skipped entirely because that branch was not taken. If greet had instead been called with an empty string, name would be falsy, and the program would print Hello, stranger instead. Every indented line here is part of a block precisely because of its indentation level, not because of any braces or keywords marking the end of the block.

Python is also dynamically typed, which means a variable is not permanently locked to one data type. You could write x = 5, making x refer to an integer, and later in the same program write x = "five", and Python will not complain, because the type is a property of the value, not of the variable name itself. This is different from many compiled languages, where a variable's type is fixed when the program is written and checked before the program ever runs. Python is also described as multiparadigm, since it comfortably supports writing straightforward step-by-step procedures as well as organizing code around objects that bundle data and behavior together, both of which you will encounter later in this course.

Another part of Python's appeal, hinted at earlier, is its enormous standard library, the collection of ready-made tools that come bundled with every Python installation for tasks like reading files, handling dates, or doing math beyond basic arithmetic, often summarized with the phrase batteries included. Combined with readable syntax and dynamic typing, this is a major reason Python shows up so often in fields as different as web development, scientific research, and introductory computer science courses. Because Python code still has to become machine instructions somehow, exactly how a Python program goes from readable source code like the example above to something the CPU can execute is the topic of the next chapter, where you will learn about the Python interpreter.
